excerpt: Writing an email somebody answers: the subject line that says the ask, the first line that does the work, and the length that gets a reply.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to write an email that somebody answers. You will write a subject line that states the ask, put the request in the first line, and keep it short enough to read on a phone.
People answer emails that are easy to answer. Most unanswered messages are not ignored out of rudeness; they are long, vague, or asking for three things at once.
Before you start

items: One message you need to send this week.
Five minutes.
The name of the person who can actually answer.

body.text: The subject line

items: Say what the email is about, and what you want, in six words.
Examples: quote for shop sign, please confirm Thursday, request for transcript.
Include a date or a reference if one exists.
Avoid words like urgent, which get filtered by some inboxes and ignored by others.
Do not leave it blank, since a blank subject is often treated as spam.
If you reply to a thread, change the subject when the topic changes.

body.text: You will see the subject list in an inbox show the first few words of each, so the ask at the front is what gets read. A subject that ends in a question mark tends to be opened first.

body.alt: An inbox list with clear subject lines beside each message.
body.caption: The subject line is the whole first impression. Six words with the ask inside them beat a clever phrase.

body.text: It looks like a polite paragraph is the best way to open. Busy people decide from the subject and the first line, and the rest is read only if those work.
The body, in four lines

items: Line one: who you are, in six words, if they may not remember.
Line two: what you want, in one sentence.
Line three: the one piece of information they need to decide.
Line four: what happens next, and by when.
Add an attachment only when it is named in the body.
Finish with your name and phone number, not a long signature.

body.text: A four-line email will show on one phone screen, which is where most recipients read it. Anything below the first screen is read later, and later is often never.

The sent list will show the message with the subject line beside it, which is the last place to check before you wait. If the subject reads like a heading rather than a question, rewrite it and send it again.

body.alt: An inbox with a small number of messages, each marked as handled.
body.caption: An inbox that is cleared daily is one where a clear message stands out. Short emails make that possible for both sides.

body.text: One ask per email
If you need three things, send three emails, or number them in a short list. A list of five questions usually gets an answer to two.

items: Number your questions, so a reply can follow the numbers.
Put the most important question first, since it will be answered first.
Say when you need the answer, and why.
Offer a default, such as I will proceed on Friday if I hear nothing.
Avoid asking for a meeting and information in the same message.
Keep the thread for one subject, so it can be found later.

body.text: None of this needs a formal tone. Plain words, short sentences, and a clear ask read as professional, and they get answered more often.
Do not worry about sounding blunt. A short email with a thank you at the start or the end is polite, and length is not the same as courtesy.
When nobody replies

items: Wait three working days before following up, unless the matter has a deadline.
Reply in the same thread, with two lines and the original ask repeated.
Try a different channel after one follow-up, such as a phone call.
Check the sent folder, since the message sometimes never left.
Look for a bounce message, which names the address that failed.
Ask somebody else in the organisation if the first person is away.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix, and each is quicker than rewriting the email.

items: You sent it to the wrong person: forward it with one line of apology and the correct ask.
You attached the wrong file: send the right one at once, and say which is correct.
You forgot the subject: reply to your own email with the subject added.
It was marked as spam: remove the links and the capital letters, and send again.
The reply misunderstands the ask: answer with the question repeated in one line.
You wrote a long email: cut it to four lines before sending, since nothing is lost by cutting.

body.text: Practice
Rewrite one message today, using the four lines.

items: Choose an email you must send.
Write a six-word subject with the ask in it.
Cut the body to four lines.
Number any questions, and put the important one first.
Read it once on a phone screen before sending.

body.text: You can now write a message that moves. In the next lesson you will keep notes you can still use in a year.

excerpt: A note-taking habit that survives a year: the one page per topic, the date in the corner, and the search that finds it again.

body.text: This lesson sets up notes you can still use in a year. You will keep one page per topic, put the date on it, and write in a way that searches well. The habit takes five minutes a day.
Notes fail for two reasons: they are written for the moment rather than for later, and they are stored where they cannot be found. Both are fixed by a simple system.
Before you start

items: A notebook, or a notes app on the phone.
One thing you learned this week.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: One page per topic

items: Start a new page for each topic, rather than one long stream.
Write the topic at the top, in the words you would search for.
Put the date in the corner, so an old note can be judged.
Add the source, such as a page or a video title.
Keep the page open for additions, rather than starting again each time.
When the page fills, start a second page with the same title and a number.

body.text: You will see the notebook fill with titles you recognise, which is the difference between a notebook and a diary. A diary records the day, and a notebook records the knowledge.

body.alt: A notebook open on a desk with a dated page and a clear title.
body.caption: Title at the top, date in the corner, source at the bottom. Three habits that make a note usable a year later.

body.text: It looks like notes should be a record of everything. A page that records everything is read by nobody, and three useful lines beat a transcript.
Write for the person you will be
Write as if the reader has forgotten the context, because in a year that reader is you.

items: Write the steps as commands, so they can be followed again.
Note the exact menu names, since those are what you will search for.
Write one line on why a step matters, not only what it was.
Mark the parts you did not understand with a question mark.
Circle the one thing you would do differently next time.
Leave a margin, so a correction can be added without rewriting.

body.text: A note with the menu names in it will be searchable. A note that says press the button will be useless in three months, when you cannot remember which button.

body.alt: A phone notes app showing several dated notes with titles.
body.caption: Titles that read like questions, and dates that tell you whether the note is still true. The search box does the rest.

body.text: Finding it again

items: Use the same word for the same thing every time, which is what makes search work.
Name notes with the thing, not the day, such as printing a sheet to fit.
Keep one index page listing the titles you have started.
Search for the menu name rather than the idea, since the menu name is exact.
For paper, keep a page at the front as an index, with page numbers.
Review the index once a month, and cross out what is finished.

body.text: None of this needs a paid app. A single text file with headings and dates searches as well as any subscription, and it opens on any device.
Do not worry about the notes looking untidy. An untidy page you can find beats a neat page you cannot.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a correction, and none of them means starting a new notebook.

items: You cannot find the note: search for the menu name, not the topic.
The notes are in four places: choose one place, and move the rest into it this month.
The note has no date: add the date you think it was, marked as approximate.
A note is out of date: write the new version above it, with today's date.
You stopped writing for a month: restart with one page, not a catch-up.
The handwriting is unreadable: type the important page, which takes ten minutes.

body.text: Practice
Write one page properly, and add it to an index.

items: Choose something you learned this week.
Write the title at the top and the date in the corner.
Write the steps as commands, with the menu names.
Add the source and one question you still have.
Add the title to your index page.

body.text: You can now keep what you learn. In the next lesson you will build a pivot table and read it without help.

excerpt: Building a pivot table from a clean list, choosing the rows and values, and the three checks that stop a summary telling the wrong story.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to build a pivot table and read it correctly. You will prepare a clean list, drag the fields into place, and run three checks that stop a summary from being misleading.
A pivot table summarises a long list without formulas. It takes one column and counts or adds another, grouping the rows as you choose.
Before you start

items: A list with a header row and no blank rows inside it.
A spreadsheet, on a computer rather than a phone.
About thirty minutes.

body.text: Clean the list first

items: One header per column, with no merged cells.
No blank rows or columns inside the data.
Dates in a date format, not typed as text.
Amounts as numbers, without a naira sign inside the cell.
One row per record, so a sale is one row and not three.
Categories spelled the same way, since food and Food become two groups.

body.text: You will see the pivot table fail in strange ways when the list is untidy, and every one of those failures comes from the data rather than the tool.

body.alt: A spreadsheet showing a pivot table summarising sales by category.
body.caption: Rows down the left, values in the middle. The summary is quick because the list underneath is tidy.

body.text: It looks like a pivot table needs formulas. It builds them for you, which is why a wrong total usually means the source data is wrong.
Build it in four moves

items: Click one cell inside the list.
Choose Insert, then Pivot table, and accept the suggested range.
Drag the category field into Rows.
Drag the amount field into Values, and check it says Sum rather than Count.
Add a date field to Columns if you want a month by month view.
Rename the sheet so it is clear what the summary covers.

body.text: The panel on the right will show four areas: rows, columns, values, and filters. Fields move between them by dragging, and the table redraws at once.

The summary screen will show the categories down the left and the totals on the right, with a grand total at the bottom. Double-click any figure and the rows behind it open in a second sheet, which is how you check a number you doubt.

body.alt: A pivot table field panel with fields being dragged into rows and values.
body.caption: Rows, columns, values, filters. A field in the wrong area gives a correct but useless answer.

body.text: Three checks before you trust it
A summary that is wrong is worse than no summary, because it looks finished.

items: Check the row count against the source, since a filter may be hiding rows.
Check the grand total against a plain sum of the amount column.
Check the date range, because a partial month makes every comparison false.
Check whether blank categories were grouped as empty, which often hides a problem.
Refresh the table after adding rows, since it does not update by itself.
Write one sentence under the table saying what it covers.

body.text: None of this needs an add-on or a paid feature. Pivot tables are in every spreadsheet app, including the free ones.
Do not worry about the size of the list. A pivot table handles thousands of rows, and the habit of checking totals works at any size.
Reading it honestly

items: Look for the largest group first, since that is where the money is.
Look for a group that is small but growing, which is often the finding.
Compare two periods, rather than reading one column alone.
Sort by value rather than alphabetically, which makes the pattern visible.
Question a total that looks too round, since a mistake often produces one.
Keep the file with the list and the table together, so the numbers can be checked.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a data problem, and each has a plain fix.

items: The total is too low: some amounts are stored as text. Retype one and watch the total move.
A category appears twice: the spelling differs, or a space was typed. Fix the list.
The table shows Count instead of Sum: change the value setting to Sum.
Rows are missing: a filter is applied on the source, or blank rows split the range.
New rows are not counted: refresh the table, which is one click.
The dates will not group by month: they are text. Convert the column to a date format.

body.text: Practice
Build one table from a list you already have.

items: Check the list has one header row and no gaps.
Insert a pivot table and put a category in Rows.
Put an amount in Values, and set it to Sum.
Compare the grand total with a plain sum.
Write one sentence saying what the table covers and its date range.

body.text: You can now summarise a long list in a minute. In the next lesson you will look up health information without being misled.

excerpt: Using the internet for health information without being frightened: the sources worth reading, the claims to ignore, and when to see a person.

body.text: This lesson is about looking up health information online without being misled. You will learn which sources are worth reading, which claims to ignore, and the point at which a person rather than a page is needed.
The internet is good at explaining a condition and bad at diagnosing one. It can tell you what a word means and cannot tell you what is wrong with you.
Before you start

items: A question you actually have, in one sentence.
A browser, and a clinic number if you have one.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Sources worth reading

items: A national health service page, which explains conditions in plain words.
The World Health Organization's pages, which are written for the public.
A teaching hospital's patient information section.
A clinic or insurer's page, which often names the doctor who wrote it.
A pharmacist, who is free to ask and knows about medicines.
Your own clinic's number, which is worth saving in contacts.

body.text: You will see a good page name the author and the date it was reviewed, usually at the bottom. A page with no author and no date is a page nobody is accountable for.

A clinic's booking page will show a phone number and a list of times, with the clinic's name at the top. If there is no address and no number, keep looking, since a page that cannot lead you to a person cannot help you.

body.alt: A phone showing a clinic booking page with a phone number and a date picker.
body.caption: A booking page with a real phone number. When a page leads to a person, it is more useful than one that leads to a shop.

body.text: It looks like a page with more detail is more reliable. Detail is quick to write, and a named author and a review date are the harder signals to fake.
Claims to ignore

items: Anything promising a cure in a fixed number of days.
A remedy that also treats several unrelated conditions.
Testimonials instead of evidence, especially with photographs.
A message that says doctors are hiding this from you.
Anything sold through a chat account with a personal name.
A page that asks you to stop taking prescribed medicine.

body.text: None of these are automatically false in every case. Together they describe a pattern that sells rather than explains, and the pattern is what to avoid.

body.alt: A person speaking to a health worker on a video call at a desk.
body.caption: A video consultation with a named clinic is still a person. Ask for the name and the registration before the call.

body.text: Reading without panic
Health pages list every possible symptom, including the rare ones, and reading them at midnight makes any symptom feel serious.

items: Read one page, not ten, since ten pages multiply the worst cases.
Write your question down before you search.
Look for the section on when to see a doctor, and read that first.
Ignore the rare conditions until a professional mentions them.
Note the answers you found, and take them to the appointment.
Do not search again after eleven at night, which is when fear does the reading.

body.text: Do not worry about having looked things up. A patient with written questions gets a better appointment than one who is trying to remember them.
When to see a person

items: Pain that is severe, sudden, or getting worse.
A fever that lasts more than a few days.
Any difficulty breathing, or chest pain.
A symptom that frightens you, whatever a page says.
A medicine question, which a pharmacist can answer today.
Anything involving a child, a pregnancy, or a long-term condition.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is about a decision rather than a technical fault, and each has a plain answer.

items: You bought a product online: stop using it, and tell your clinic what it contained.
You stopped a prescription: restart only on advice from a professional, and call today.
You are frightened by what you read: write the question down, and call the clinic.
The advice conflicts: trust the source that names an author and a date.
A relative is sharing a cure: ask for the clinic that recommends it, and wait.
You cannot reach a clinic: ask a pharmacist, who is the nearest professional.

body.text: Practice
Do one search properly, on a small question.

items: Write one question in a sentence.
Search it, and open only a page with a named author.
Read the section on when to see a doctor.
Note two facts, with the source and the date.
Save your clinic's number in contacts.

body.text: You can now read health information without being ruled by it. In the next lesson you will build the habit of learning one new thing each month.

excerpt: Keeping your skills current without chasing every new tool: the monthly hour, the one thing to learn, and how to tell a real change from noise.

body.text: This lesson is about keeping your skills current without chasing every new tool. You will set a monthly hour, choose one thing to learn, and tell the difference between a real change and noise.
Tools change constantly and skills change slowly. The habit that keeps you employable is learning one useful thing regularly, rather than reacting to every announcement.
Before you start

items: A calendar or a notebook.
One hour a month, at a fixed time.
About fifteen minutes to plan.

body.text: The monthly hour

items: Choose a fixed day, such as the first Saturday morning.
Write it in the calendar as an appointment, not a hope.
Choose one thing, from a list you keep during the month.
Practise it on something real, not on a tutorial file.
Write a page of notes at the end, in your usual format.
Add the next thing to the list, and close the laptop.

body.text: You will see twelve pages of notes after a year, each one a skill you can name in an interview. That is more than most people produce by watching videos they never finish.

body.alt: A shelf of notebooks with dates on the spines.
body.caption: One notebook per year, dated on the spine. The shelf is the evidence, and evidence is what gets recalled at an interview.

body.text: It looks like you must learn everything new to stay relevant. Most announcements change the packaging, and the skill underneath is the same one you already have.
Real change or noise

items: Real change: your current tool stops doing a job you need.
Real change: employers in your field ask for the same thing in five adverts.
Real change: a client asks for it, and pays for it.
Noise: a new version with a new name and the same buttons.
Noise: one person online saying everything else is dead.
Noise: a course that promises a salary in six weeks.

body.text: None of this means ignoring new tools. It means letting the adverts and the clients decide the order, rather than the loudest announcement.
Do not worry about falling behind. Behind is measured against your field, and your field moves more slowly than the timeline suggests.

body.alt: A laptop screen showing a new tool being tried with a notebook beside it.
body.caption: One tool, tried on real work, with notes. Twenty tools watched and never used teach nothing.

body.text: Learn it on real work
A skill practised on a real task is remembered; a skill practised on a sample file is not.

items: Take a task you already do, and do it in the new tool.
Compare the result with your usual method, in time and in quality.
Keep the new method only if it wins on one of the two.
Write the steps in the same place as your other notes.
Teach it to one person, which is the test of understanding.
Add it to your CV only after you have used it for real.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is common, and each costs an hour rather than a career.

items: You skipped three months: restart with one hour, not a catch-up month.
The tool was useless: write one line about why, which saves you trying it again.
You learned nothing usable: the task was too small. Choose one from your actual work.
You feel behind your colleagues: ask what they use daily, which is usually less than they claim.
A course promised a job: check the adverts, since employers hire and courses teach.
You cannot find the hour: take it from scrolling, which is where the hour usually is.

body.text: Practice
Book the hour, and choose the first thing.

items: Put a monthly hour in the calendar, with an alarm.
Start a list of things you have wanted to learn.
Choose the first one, and a real task to practise it on.
Write the notes page at the end of the hour.
Book the next month before you close the laptop.

body.text: You can now keep learning without chasing. In the next lesson you will bank without data, using the codes on your phone.
